description_full: Apartment Investment and Management Company is a diversified real estate company primarily focused on value add and opportunistic investments, targeting the U.S. multifamily sector. Aimco's mission is to make real estate investments where outcomes are enhanced through our human capital so that substantial value is created for investors, teammates, and the communities in which we operate. Aimco is traded on the New York Stock Exchange as AIV. Apartment Investment and Management Company was incorporated in 1975 in Maryland, USA.
ceo_bio: Mr. Wesley William Powell | President, CEO & Director | Age 45 | Compensation: $7.8M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 50 people. Revenue per employee of $2.8M ranks in the above the sector median among Real Estate peers, declining at 13%/yr — weakening productivity. Stock-based compensation of $118K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: Apartment Investment and Manage is a micro-cap real estate business with a $239M market cap on $138M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -10% over the past three years and -18% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 1% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The company is burning through $92M of cash, and without positive owner earnings any valuation rests on hope rather than evidence.
Accruals are elevated at +32.2% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 0.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Insiders hold 2.4% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 31% operating margin runs 9pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+15.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 32% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 74% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 24% and a beta of 0.94, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.43 vs 5y 0.93), so read it loosely.
About $3.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 54% in the 2020 crash, 30% in the 2022 bear market and 83% in 2008.
val: The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 100%), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on P/E 8.2 vs 23.6, richer on EV/EBITDA 67.7 vs 16.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 113% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of -38.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.9% (vs the 8% bar).
prof: ROIC of 1% falls short of the cost of capital of 7.3%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.29).
It burns cash (FCF margin -66%), or -70% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is a concern: cash conversion of only 0.01x and high accruals (+32.2% of assets).
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is -66%.
ROE of 151% is amplified by 4.6x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 5pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.4x net debt to EBITDA ($394.9M of cash against $738.6M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 0.7x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.24 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The value-trap profile is elevated (60/100); see the breakdown below.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -10.1% over 3 years, -1.8% over 5 years and -17.8% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 23%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 0.8% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of -29.9% a year over five years.
Capex runs 1.7x depreciation (71.9% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is -72, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.4%, and institutions hold 78%.
The share count has shrunk 1.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
